verdicts.reading: Quantitative (D16/D10 rule): global console game sales reach US$23 billion in 2006, on the definition of the report's own Figure 3 (Screen Digest, global console game sales).
verdicts.reason: The definitional gap both graders named is narrower than they thought: the chapter's Figure 3 is titled 'Global console game sales' and sourced to Screen Digest, 'Games Software Publishing - Strategies for Success' (November 2005), so the $23bn is Screen Digest's console game (software) series. No public 2006 actual on that definition was found: Screen Digest figures sit in paid reports; US-only NPD figures and all-platform retail totals (hardware plus software, PC, online) are different quantities (D23). Looked for: Screen Digest 2006/2007 console software press figures, DFC Intelligence, ESA/NPD, PwC outlook. One web search, plus the Deloitte PDF opened. Stays ungradable.
verdicts.fetched: Deloitte Media Predictions 2006 PDF (Internet Archive), page 8, Figure 3 caption and source.

evidence.title: Deloitte TMT Trends: Predictions 2006, Media, 'Video game sector enters next generation'
evidence.shows: The $23bn sits beside Figure 3 'Global console game sales' ($m, USA/Japan/Europe/ROW, 2000-2006), source Screen Digest, Games Software Publishing, November 2005: the forecast is Screen Digest's console software series.

verdicts.reading: Possibility claim: 'With sufficient collaboration and focus, the mobile industry could make 2008 the year in which machines finally become a driver of growth.'
verdicts.reason: A measure exists, so not ungradable: Berg Insight counts cellular M2M connections (81.4 million at end-2010, up 46% year on year, so about 56 million at end-2009), against 662 million net new mobile subscriptions worldwide in 2008 (ITU, cited by grader B). Machines were at most a few percent of 2008 subscription growth, so read as a forecast it would be a miss. But the sentence is a conditional possibility: hedge word 'could', conditioned on 'sufficient collaboration and focus', and the chapter's bottom line frames machines as 'the major opportunity', not an expected outcome. Under D30 (and D27) a possibility-only claim is unfalsifiable: both outcomes agree with it. This differs from the 'may' claims graded elsewhere in this source (for example 2009-006), which state an expected outcome without a condition.
verdicts.fetched: Deloitte Telecommunications Predictions 2008 PDF chapter (Internet Archive); Telecompaper report of Berg Insight's M2M count.

verdicts.reading: In 2008 more GPS-enabled phones ship, but beyond the initial novelty their owners rarely use GPS.
verdicts.reason: The graded part is usage frequency among GPS-phone owners. The nearest public measure is comScore M:Metrics (July 2008): 8% of US and 3% of European mobile subscribers accessed maps on the phone in the three months to May 2008, US up 82% and Europe up 49% year on year, mostly via the browser and for driving directions. Its base is all subscribers, not GPS-phone owners, the leading US device (the original iPhone) had no GPS, and it gives reach, not frequency; using it would grade a different quantity (D23). Looked for 2008 comScore, Nielsen Mobile, Berg Insight and J.D. Power usage figures among GPS-handset owners; none found in public. Stays ungradable.
verdicts.fetched: Deloitte Telecommunications Predictions 2008 chapter (Internet Archive); comScore press release July 2008.

verdicts.reading: In 2009 digital litigation (lawsuits over digital products, personal data, digital rights and IP infringement) proves recession-proof or counter-cyclical.
verdicts.reason: Both graders read the claim as e-discovery revenue. The chapter is about the volume of lawsuits over digital matters (privacy, product claims, RSI, IP and copyright class actions), not about electronic discovery services, so e-discovery revenue is a different quantity (D23). For the record, on the graders' reading the Socha-Gelbmann surveys give 2007 commercial e-discovery revenue of $2.794bn (with a pre-recession projection of $4.051bn for 2009) and 2009 revenue of about $2.8bn: flat rather than falling, which a 'recession-proof' reading would call a hit and a 'kept growing' reading a stall; that reading is not graded. No public series counts digital-related litigation across these case types for 2008 and 2009. Looked for: Socha-Gelbmann public results 2008 to 2010, litigation trend surveys, patent and copyright filing counts (each covers only one slice). Stays ungradable.
verdicts.fetched: Deloitte Technology Predictions 2009 chapter (Internet Archive); Socha-Gelbmann 2008 survey public results and 2009 survey table of contents (Internet Archive); Comstock's article citing the 2010 Socha-Gelbmann survey.

verdicts.reading: State of affairs (D30): in 2009 enterprise social networking grows, but its adoption stays within a minority of (leading-edge) firms.
verdicts.reason: Grader A named the right measure (McKinsey's 2009 Web 2.0 survey) but could not open it. Opened via the Internet Archive: the survey (fielded June 2009, about 1,700 executives) shows, in Exhibit 2, internal use of social networking by 42% of respondents at companies reporting benefits and 30% at companies reporting none, among only the 1,032 respondents whose companies use Web 2.0 internally; across all respondents that is well under half. McKinsey's 2010 survey reports 'significant increases' in the share of companies using social networking, to 40% (internal and external use), so 2009 was below 40% and rising. Growth in 2009 and adoption by a minority both held as stated. Hit. Grader B's Inc. 500 figure measured external social media, not internal networks.
verdicts.fetched: McKinsey 2009 survey page and Exhibit 2 image (mckinsey.com via Internet Archive, 2023 capture); McKinsey Quarterly 2009 original page (Internet Archive); McKinsey 2010 survey page (Internet Archive).

verdicts.reading: State of affairs (D30): in 2009 the biggest driver of Internet radio listening is the portable, easy-to-use WiFi radio set.
verdicts.reason: Two public measures, in the two largest markets for the chapter's argument. UK: Ofcom's Communications Market Report 2010 (Figure 1.2) puts WiFi radio take-up at 2% of individuals in Q1 2010, while 15% listened to radio via the internet monthly, so sets were a small share of the audience. US: the Arbitron/Edison Infinite Dial 2010 has weekly online radio at 17% in both the early-2009 and early-2010 surveys (no growth over 2009), listening going to Internet-only services (Pandora) and computers, and a radio-like Internet radio device appearing only as an interest item (18% 'very interested'). WiFi sets were neither the biggest impetus nor a visible one in 2009. Miss. 'May' is Deloitte's usual pre-2010 voice for an expected outcome in this source and is graded as such (as in 2009-006).
verdicts.fetched: Deloitte Media Predictions 2009 chapter (Internet Archive); Infinite Dial 2010 slides (Edison Research PDF via Internet Archive); Ofcom CMR 2010 PDF.
